events.text:
Direct answer: Britannica (1771–1797) says a magnet attracts iron because the magnet induces magnetism in the iron, and the attraction is a "secondary phenomenon" — the consequence of the "proper disposition of the induced magnetism" in the iron. Wikipedia says attraction is produced by a magnetic field, and that ferromagnetic materials like iron are attracted because of the magnetic moments of their atoms' orbiting electrons and quantum-mechanical spin — i.e., electromagnetism and quantum mechanics, which Britannica has no concept of.

Uncertainty: the Britannica–Wikipedia match is uncertain (uncertain_match: true; rerank logit −4.37, margin 0.31), and the Britannica text is 18th-century OCR with long-s errors, so I verified the key quote against the page scan before quoting it.

Evidence:
- Britannica [B:756:0], entry "MAGNETISM" (p. 129, Supplement Vol. II Part 1), verified against the scan: "a piece of magnetic iron is always attracted by a magnet"; "this attraction of the loadstone for iron, or this tendency of iron to the loadstone, is a secondary phenomenon, and is the consequence of the proper disposition of the induced magnetism." The entry explains magnetization by induction/contact (tempered steel and iron bars acquire magnetism by juxtaposition; the effect dissipates after the inducing magnet is removed) and attributes the Earth's magnetism to "a certain degree of oxydation, and perhaps some other positive yet unknown" cause. It has no concept of electromagnetism, electrons, or atoms.
- Wikipedia [W:19716:1352239981], "Magnetism": "Magnetism is the class of physical attributes that occur through a magnetic field... Because both electric currents and magnetic moments of elementary particles give rise to a magnetic field... The most familiar effects occur in ferromagnetic materials, which are strongly attracted by magnetic fields... Only a few substances are ferromagnetic; the most common ones are iron, cobalt, nickel, and their alloys." And: "The magnetic properties of materials are mainly due to the magnetic moments of their atoms' orbiting electrons" and "intrinsic magnetic dipoles arising from quantum-mechanical spin"; "magnetism is one of two aspects of electromagnetism," governed by Maxwell's equations.

Comparison (from the saved pair's drift block): the shared point "iron is attracted by a magnet" is tagged enduring; Britannica's claim that magnetism "arises from the proper disposition of induced magnetism in iron" is tagged superseded by Wikipedia's atomic electron-moment explanation; 25% of checked claims are superseded, 37.5% dropped (including Britannica's watch-spring steel and Brook Taylor claims), and Wikipedia-only topics include paramagnetism/diamagnetism/antiferromagnetism, Maxwell's equations, and the quantum-mechanical origin.

Inference: the difference is not just wording but a change in knowledge — Britannica explains attraction via induced magnetism and an unknown cause for terrestrial magnetism, while Wikipedia explains it via electron magnetic moments, spin, and quantum mechanics within electromagnetism.

Sources: [B:756:0] (Britannica MAGNETISM entry, row 756; verified against scan 756-full.jpg, image_sha256 33eb91fc...), [W:19716:1352239981] (Wikipedia "Magnetism", revision 1352239981).

final_text:
Direct answer: Britannica (1771–1797) says a magnet attracts iron because the magnet induces magnetism in the iron, and the attraction is a "secondary phenomenon" — the consequence of the "proper disposition of the induced magnetism" in the iron. Wikipedia says attraction is produced by a magnetic field, and that ferromagnetic materials like iron are attracted because of the magnetic moments of their atoms' orbiting electrons and quantum-mechanical spin — i.e., electromagnetism and quantum mechanics, which Britannica has no concept of.

Uncertainty: the Britannica–Wikipedia match is uncertain (uncertain_match: true; rerank logit −4.37, margin 0.31), and the Britannica text is 18th-century OCR with long-s errors, so I verified the key quote against the page scan before quoting it.

Evidence:
- Britannica [B:756:0], entry "MAGNETISM" (p. 129, Supplement Vol. II Part 1), verified against the scan: "a piece of magnetic iron is always attracted by a magnet"; "this attraction of the loadstone for iron, or this tendency of iron to the loadstone, is a secondary phenomenon, and is the consequence of the proper disposition of the induced magnetism." The entry explains magnetization by induction/contact (tempered steel and iron bars acquire magnetism by juxtaposition; the effect dissipates after the inducing magnet is removed) and attributes the Earth's magnetism to "a certain degree of oxydation, and perhaps some other positive yet unknown" cause. It has no concept of electromagnetism, electrons, or atoms.
- Wikipedia [W:19716:1352239981], "Magnetism": "Magnetism is the class of physical attributes that occur through a magnetic field... Because both electric currents and magnetic moments of elementary particles give rise to a magnetic field... The most familiar effects occur in ferromagnetic materials, which are strongly attracted by magnetic fields... Only a few substances are ferromagnetic; the most common ones are iron, cobalt, nickel, and their alloys." And: "The magnetic properties of materials are mainly due to the magnetic moments of their atoms' orbiting electrons" and "intrinsic magnetic dipoles arising from quantum-mechanical spin"; "magnetism is one of two aspects of electromagnetism," governed by Maxwell's equations.

Comparison (from the saved pair's drift block): the shared point "iron is attracted by a magnet" is tagged enduring; Britannica's claim that magnetism "arises from the proper disposition of induced magnetism in iron" is tagged superseded by Wikipedia's atomic electron-moment explanation; 25% of checked claims are superseded, 37.5% dropped (including Britannica's watch-spring steel and Brook Taylor claims), and Wikipedia-only topics include paramagnetism/diamagnetism/antiferromagnetism, Maxwell's equations, and the quantum-mechanical origin.

Inference: the difference is not just wording but a change in knowledge — Britannica explains attraction via induced magnetism and an unknown cause for terrestrial magnetism, while Wikipedia explains it via electron magnetic moments, spin, and quantum mechanics within electromagnetism.
